editorial.headline: Rice and Palawija Wholesale: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale trade in rice, corn, paddy, wheat and rice planting material is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but PMA registration in Bali is blocked by a permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, registration of this activity in Bali is not possible today. That is the practical Bali position even though the national PMA setting is open to full foreign ownership. The difference is explicit in the record: Bali blocks the activity at the risk-class level under a province-wide, permanent moratorium. The scope itself, however, is a defined wholesale activity covering the outputs of rice and palawija cultivation.

The stated subject includes rice, corn, paddy or unhusked rice (*gabah*), wheat, rice seed, rice seedlings and palawija. In clear English, palawija refers here to secondary food crops. The inclusion of both harvested products and rice planting material gives the activity a precise commercial frame, while keeping it within wholesale trade. Its identity rests on the named agricultural products in the official scope, rather than on a broad, undefined idea of agricultural business.

The record opens this activity to micro, small, medium and large scales. It is therefore not reserved for one size of undertaking: the same stated wholesale subject is recognised from Mikro through Besar. That breadth is an important part of the classification’s formal picture. It says that the activity may be registered across the listed business-scale range, while the product scope remains anchored in rice, palawija and the specifically named commodities and planting materials.

Nationally, PMA is TERBUKA and the maximum foreign ownership is 100%. In plain terms, the record places no national foreign-equity ceiling below full ownership for this activity. Its stated basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali changes the practical result: at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, and Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA. That island-wide rule is described as permanent, and the record attributes this block to the Bali moratorium referenced in May 2026. National openness is therefore real, but it does not create a PMA registration path in Bali.
